#897. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

#894. Bo Derek Gives Rare Details on Ranch Life With Husband John Corbett

Bo Derek—who turned 70 on Nov. 20—shared the sweet ways husband John Corbett spoils her while giving insight into her marriage with the Sex and the City star.

Bo Derek couldn't help but wonder what John Corbett would do for her 70th birthday.

The Bolero actress gave rare insight into the couple's life on a 110-acre ranch near Santa Barbara, Calif., while detailing their plans to ring in her milestone year on Nov. 20.

“He’s a great gift giver," Derek told People, recalling one such special gift from her husband. “I have a friend with a company. He’s very successful, and he’s starting a new company. And John went and got me shares in his company. It’s so much fun. I am not a wheeler dealer or a trader by any means. It’s all just algebra to me."

But more than any present, Derek appreciates the gift of Corbett's companionship.

“He keeps me laughing," she shared of the Sex and the City alum. "He’s very youthful, enthusiastic."

So much so that the model doesn't need a big party with dozens of friends.

“If you have 20 or 30 people, you’re just running around—‘Hi, what do you need? Can I get you a drink?’” she said. “I always felt a little empty after a big party.”

That's why Corbett, 65, came up with an idea that would have Carrie Bradshaw quaking in her Manolo Blahnik boots.

“He said, ‘I don’t care how many weeks it takes. Why don’t we invite a friend or two at a time and have meaningful dinners with them?’" Derek said. “That’s probably what I’ll do this year, because I love it."

Limiting their social engagements isn't the only way the pair—who met in 2002 and married in 2020—maintain a quiet life on their coastal farm. As she explained, they also prefer to stay home to spend time with their two German shepherds.

“When we first met, he didn’t want to have a girlfriend with a dog because they just require too much time. You’re just off going off having fun, and you got to rush back to the dog,” she told the outlet. “And now I can’t get him to go anywhere with me because he doesn’t want to leave the dogs.”

But fortunately, that take hasn't landed him in the doghouse, as Derek revealed she's also fond of her man's best friend, adding, “It’s not fun for him unless the dogs are with us and it’s great that we share that.”

Read on for what other celebrities have credited as the secrets behind their long-lasting marriages.

"I never thought that I would laugh this much in my marriage. That is such a fundamental ingredient of who you are, this insistence on joy," Hermann detailed to his bride of their partnership of over 20 years in Marlo Thomas and Phil Donahue's 2020 book What Makes a Marriage Last. "And I think what sustains our marriage is that I know you love me in spite of who I am, and that is the definition of grace."Seeking out that happiness is key. Even after a particularly robust argument, "One of us will test the waters with a joke—about the very thing we were fighting about," Herman shared of life with the Law & Order: SVU star. "It's like one of us says, 'I'm not saying I was wrong, and I'm not still insisting I was entirely right, but can we at least inch our way back toward the place where we caught at stuff together?' Once that happens, it's a pretty good sign that things are on their way to getting patched up."

They've avoided need for any major renovation by sticking to the same advice they got in premarital counseling ahead of their 2003 vows. Even five kids in, Tuesday date nights are a must and they've held off on purchasing a TV, instead finding other ways to connect. But if Chip were to offer any tip to follow, it'd be to pursue the person you love "like a hornet." Some two decades in, he said, he still feels like the guy hoping to get a second date. "I'm not saying she'd never cheat on me," he explained, "but it's not going to be because I never told her I loved her or because I didn't send her flowers or I forgot our anniversary."

"My first piece of advice is not to take advice from celebrities," Bacon joked of his 36-year union. It's as succinct as their other go-to, "Keep the fights clean and the sex dirty," a phrase developed specifically to end any further chatter about their marriage. Truthfully, though, they make it a point not to let arguments linger, rarely digging in for the sake of the victory. "Honestly, we don't like to fight, so when we actually are in an argument, we're both looking for a solution," The Closer actress explained to Thomas and Donahue. "For the most part we're struggling to get back to everything being okay, because it sucks to fight." Because, when it comes down to it, she continued, "There is no Plan B. No matter what, we want to work it out."

Over 37 years into marriage, the actors have mastered the art of fighting fair. "Tracy and I don't pick scabs," explained the Family Ties alum. "In some marriages, people look at their partner and see vulnerability and they just can't help but go after that vulnerability, like it's a sport or something. We don't do that." That's not to say they don't have arguments. "If I've said something stupid, I have the tendency to want to take it back and make it all okay," he said. "But that doesn't really work." Instead, he follows her lead and tries to give her space. She, in turn, offers up understanding: "Sometimes you just have to say to yourself, 'You know what? He said something schmucky and it made me feel bad. But he's a good person and I'm going to give him the benefit of the doubt that he didn't realize that what he said hurt my feelings.'"

"He still makes me laugh more than any human being," Curtis said about the Waiting for Guffman director on Today in December 2024, ahead of the couple's 40th wedding anniversary, adding jokingly, "and I'm sure there's something about me that he likes. I don't know what it is, but I'm sure there's something."

"I think one of the things that has kept us together all of these years is that we both define relationships as something that's relatively indefinable," the How I Met Your Mother alum said. Through 21 years of career shifts (actor-chef Burtka released his cookbook Life Is a Party in 2019), parenting twins Gideon and Harper and dealing with tough times, "Marriage never stays the same," explained Harris. "When you have sex with the same person over and over, it gets redundant, and so you try different things. Then one day you don't like each other, and suddenly you're not attracted to each other, so you have to figure out how to be reattracted to them—but in a different way because you're aging."Eventually, he continued, you find yourself more attracted to their soul. And then their body again. "It all keeps morphing," he noted. "So in a weird way, we keep falling in love with each other in different ways, over and over."

Appropriately, the comic actors believe their funniness gives them life. And not just in their 19-year union itself. "Whenever we have a good laugh," noted the Can You Ever Forgive Me? actress, "especially a crazy one, when you're like, Oh, my God, and you're almost dizzy—we always assign it a specific amount of time that it added to our lives. And I'm always adding it up. I'll say, 'Okay, that was like two months—I just got two more months to live!'"They put a time limit on disagreements as well. Citing the oft-repeated don't go to bed angry rule, Falcone, said, "I tried it once, and I realized that in the morning I had forgotten what I was mad about. You're not getting any answers if you're parsing out an argument when everybody is tired and possibly had a drink or two. I've never had the thing where you're having an argument at ten o'clock at night, and then you say, 'Well, that was good. I'm glad we got to the bottom of that. We agree. Truce signed.'"

Each having wed before they found their way to the other in 1995, they not only had to navigate a marriage, but life as step-parents to two children apiece. "There is no book that tells you how to do it, so the one thing I figured out right away is that they already have a mom—and it's not me. So what did they need from me?" the Zoey's Extraordinary Playlist actor recalled. "That's when I realized that everybody needs a cheerleader, right? There's never too many of those in your life, so that's what I'll be. I never set their boundaries, disciplined them, or tried to teach them right from wrong. They have parents who do that."The Cheers alum agreed with her stance wholeheartedly. "I think that's really wise, to offer yourself as a friend," he said. "‘I'm not going to discipline you and I'm not going to judge you. What I'm going to do is hang out with you and be there for you.' And that's what you have to do: absolutely, genuinely be there."

The moment same-sex civil unions were legalized in Britain, the music icon and the Canadian ad exec were joined together in a Dec. 21, 2005 ceremony. They repeated the process on the exact same day nine years later once they were able to legally wed. And yet the anniversary they recognize is their unexpected meeting during a 1993 weekend dinner party at the singer's Windsor, England flat, his friend having set the guest list.Every Saturday, no matter where they are in the world, together or apart, the two pen a handwritten note to each other, by the authors' count, some 1,352 letters in all. "There's something very spiritual and real about handwriting," explains Furnish, "and the cards are a chance to reflect on the week that's passed and talk about the week that's coming up." Agreed the five-time Grammy winner, "It's part of the success, I think, of a lasting relationship. Communication is the most important thing."

Having literally Secreted their 40-year marriage into existence ("Six months before I met him, I had these recurring dreams about this person I was going to marry,") they make sure their union has remained front-and-center even as their entire existence has shifted. "Marriage is a priority for both of us. And that means that we act on that and refocus when we've lost sight of the ball," she said. If the surgeon could prescribe one piece of advice, it would be to place that bond above all else. "The bottom line is this: I would do anything for her. Climb any mountain, take any bullet—in the chest, too, by the way. I might do things that justifiably make her really angry at me, but I would never let anything block me from delivering my love to her," he swore. If you appreciate how valuable marriage is to your long-term happiness, he continued, "You will never let anyone touch it."

ABC News reporter Roberts isn't always one for chit-chat. "I don't like the check-in," she explaind. "If you're calling just to say, 'So, what's up?' no, I do not like that." Everyone's favorite TV weatherman, however, is a phone guy. And after years of chafing against his frequent calls, a pal proposed something that changed her stance. "One friend said to me, 'Did you ever think that maybe he just feels comfortable when he hears your voice, because that tells him that all is right in the world?'" she recounted. "And I thought, 'That's very sweet. I'd never thought about it in that way. And if it means something to him, then it should mean something to me.'"Now, she said, "I have learned to take a breath and say, 'Sweetie, I've got some stuff going on, but what's going on with you? Great. I'm glad to hear from you. Got to go. Talk to you later. Love you.' That makes all the difference in the world to him, and it doesn't kill me for two minutes to be nice and sweet." They celebrated their 29th anniversary in September 2024.

The building blocks for their nearly 30-year union began back in their newlywed days, when any fight—one involved the Riverdale actor throwing the talk show host's ring out the window—felt like it could be it. "Early in a marriage, it's easy to let little things become big things—whether it's financial strain or career strain or you have kids and you're sleep-deprived," espoused the LIVE With Kelly and Ryan star. "But Mark taught me to walk away and take a breath. That's when you figure out that it's not a marriage-defining moment."Some hard-earned wisdom, to be sure, but now the parents of three are reaping the benefits. "Anytime you see a couple who seems truly happy, you can bet they've gone through some crazy, crazy stuff together and they've survived," he stated. "That's something to be proud of."

She's an introvert, she said, "maybe a step away from being a straight-up loner"; he's the ultimate extrovert "the mayor of everywhere," as he put it. She's a touch messy; he's "a little OCD" noted the Oscar winner. But, wed since 2003, they've long since learned to let the other do their thing. That's the advice the How to Get Away With Murder lead said she gives to all her soon-to-be-wed friends. "Marriage does not start when you walk down the aisle," she shared. "Your marriage starts when you look over at a person who you love more than anything, and there's something about him—just one character trait that makes you say to yourself, 'Oh man, that's going to drive me crazy. I don't know if I can deal with this.' And then the next minute you say, 'But you know what? I love him.' That's when your marriage starts."

You don't reach the 50-year mark in any relationship by letting disagreements drag on. Any time there's a blowup, noted the Grace and Frankie star, "Usually, I'm the one who apologizes. It's not hard because I love her and can't bear for her to feel lonely for even five minutes." Even better is when she can avoid saying she's sorry to the writer altogether. Her top takeaway, she shared, "Remember, when you're angry at your partner and say something hurtful, you will be more angry at yourself later for having said hurtful things to the person you love. You'll feel angry twice. Not good for your blood pressure, and certainly not good for your relationship."

Few things are more on brand than former New York State Supreme Court judge Jerry declaring their decades-long union works because he usually lets the Judge Judy icon win. But for his bride it's more about knowing you're not always going to like the final verdict. Their 12-year marriage dissolved in 1990 when he couldn't be the caretaker she needed following her father's death. Yet, when they got back together one year later and quickly remarried, she had no delusions that he was suddenly going to be the type to run the household or take the lead on birthday plans. "Every relationship is different, but there is a common thread of unhappiness, and that unhappiness comes from trying to make another person different from who they are. You can try, but they're always going to resent it," she explained matter-of-factly. "I don't think you should marry anyone with the expectation of changing who they are."

The Lost alum would be, well, lost without his longtime love, who he married in 1993. As he explained to E! News in April 2025, "My wife—being patient as I traipse around the world, going from job to job—she's kept our family stable. She's been fantastic."

Calling her a "very patient woman," the actor said his wife and their two sons keeps him "humble no matter what's happening."

"They shape my values," he added. "It's great to have that perspective and North Star."

#890. Ina Garten Reveals Reason She Turned Down Dancing With the Stars Offer

Food Network legend Ina Garten said she was once asked to join the Dancing With the Stars cast, but explained she declined the offer because “nobody needs to see that.”

Ina Garten will be sticking to the edible form of salsa.

While the Barefoot Contessa chef may be an expert at slicing and dicing in the kitchen, she is adamant her skills wouldn’t transfer to the ballroom.

“Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” Garten said on the Nov. 18 episode of her Happy Hour podcast. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”

Plus, the 78-year-old anticipated that her nerves would get the best of her. As she suggested, “I thought, ‘The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares.’”

(FWIW, her fellow Food Network star Giada De Laurentiis competed this season on Dancing With the Stars alongside pro partner Alan Bersten, though the pair were eliminated in week two of the competition.)

Of course, Garten’s aversion to a Viennese waltz isn’t the only honest opinion she has served up on a silver platter over the years. In fact, she has been candid about her decision to not have kids during her nearly 60-year marriage to husband Jeffrey Garten.

“It’s amazing to me that I made that decision so young, and that thank God Jeffrey was OK with it,” she recalled on a November 2025 episode of the Good Hang with Amy Poehler podcast. “I just can’t imagine my life any other way I’ve done it. I’ve done what I wanted to do. I’ve had just a wonderful time.”

Not having kids has also allowed Garten and her husband to prioritize their marriage, which she revealed in her 2024 memoir Be Ready When the Luck Happens led them to couples counseling after her burgeoning career put their relationship on the backburner.

"While I was still cooking, cleaning, shopping, managing at the store, I was doing it as a businesswoman, not a wife," she wrote in the book. "My responsibilities made it impossible for me to even think about anything else.”

However, after kneading the lumps out of their issues with hard work and therapy, Garten noted they “heard each other” better.

“Moving forward, we could be equals who took care of each other,” she added. “It wouldn’t happen overnight, but if we worked toward the same goal, we could change things together."

While Garten may not have been among the season 35 cast of Dancing With the Stars, read on to look back at who has competed throughout this season.

The 10 Things I Hate About You star had her last dance with her pro partner during Nov. 2's Disney Night.

The celebrity chef couldn't cha-cha-chop away the competition and was eliminated during the Sept. 22 episode.

What did you miss on Glee? The actor taking his musical talents to the dance floor.

Sadly, the former '90s teen heartthrob did not MMMBop his way to the top of the leaderboard on season 35. He and his pro partner were axed from the competition on Sept. 29.

The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air actress will be bringing her fresh moves to the dance floor.

Twenty years after starring in Step Up, the dancer stepped up—and out—when she got cut from the competition in a shocking Nov. 10 elimination.

The 2026 Olympic figure skater will take her skills from the ice to the ballroom.

The Team USA Paralympic track and field athlete will show off his athleticism on DWTS.

Though her sister Brooks Nader was the fifth star to be eliminated on season 33, the Love Thy Nader star said goodbye to the competition after her debut episode on Sept. 16.

The comedian, also known as Fibula on social media, is ready to earn more applause on DWTS.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star followed his wife Whitney Leavitt's footsteps after her season 34 appearance, but he bid farwell to the season 35 competition during the Sept. 15 premiere.

Though the Bachelor Nation star traded in roses for rumbas, he was sent home on Oct. 27 in a double elimination.

The Savannah Bananas baseball player stepped up to the plate, but struck out on Oct. 27 in a double elimination.

The Jimmy Kimmel Live! star was ready to learn some new moves, but his time on DWTS was cut short on Oct. 13.

Even though Summer House star had fans screaming "bravo," she was eliminated from the competition on Oct. 6.

The Love Island U.K. alum is hoping her love for DWTS doesn't betray her as she manifested this experience.

"I have a vision board and I redo it every year," she told E! News in May. "This year is the first year that I stayed at home by myself on New Year's Eve. I did not go out at all. I made myself a bowl of pasta and a glass of red wine and I redid my vision board for the year. Dancing With the Stars was already on it from the year before. However, I added five more Dancing With the Stars on the board."

#886. Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows

Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

#883. Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’

Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham

The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

Hayworth’s family was from Seville province. “I know she was a great actress but I’m afraid I have to admit I’m not one for old films,” García concedes in an even tone. “My uncles played rugby for Ciencias and practically all of them were in the national team together. They tried to get me to play with my cousins, but I was always more into football.” He was good at it too: another Spain international, the Club World Cup’s top scorer, playing for Real Madrid.

Then this summer, with opportunities limited, he joined Fulham, his introductory interview conducted in impeccable English. Having joined Madrid aged 10, he was leaving home for the first time, as Fulham’s record signing, at 22. He had the language and intelligence to embrace it. As for being uprooted, he was used to that, growing up in Argentina and Chile as well as Spain.

“From very little my parents impressed upon me the importance of study, learning languages,” García says. “I’m at Villanueva university [in Madrid]. I started with dual honours business and analytics, although that became difficult with my profession. Now it’s just business, and I’m trying to arrange with the university how best to handle it [from London]. My parents considered it fundamental to speak English and I was always at international schools.

“Every two or three years we would change city. Obviously, there would be phases when I felt: ‘Pfff, again?!’ Having to move home because of my parents’ work. But I look back and feel grateful because, seen with perspective, it gives you opportunities to meet new people, see new places, learn. I’ve always had foreign friends with whom I spoke English.”

García has been joined at Fulham by César Palacios and Manuel Ángel from Madrid’s academy. Three 22-year-olds, like your very own Erasmus course. “Nah,” García says, laughing. “I wouldn’t call it an Erasmus because we’re talking about a big, ambitious career step. We’re grateful for the trust placed in us. I’ve been pleasantly surprised by London, a huge city with people from all nationalities and cultures and Fulham fit the situation I was in, the desire to grow.

“Álvaro Arbeloa explained the project, convinced me. I’d worked with him in Madrid. He knows me perfectly, how far he can push me. Equally, I know what he wants of me. That helps … [Arbeloa] told me it was a project that it will take time but that he needed me. I’m very, very happy. It’s one of the world’s best leagues, if not the best.”

And the toughest? Is English football as wild as it looks? “Yes!” García replies. “They had told me it was demanding, hard, but …” He cracks up. “I have to admit it still surprised me. That first game against Chelsea, I finished really, really tired. It was box to box, intense, a lot of running. Bit by bit I’m adapting. The intensity and pace is very different.

“Spain is more tactical, a bit more technical. English football is pace. You can’t lose concentration for a second, not a second. Anything can happen any moment. How many Premier League games are decided late? Suddenly there’s a goal in the 90th minute and again on 93. It’s your corner and their chance. The level of concentration, that constant transition, is what most sets the Premier League apart.”

Despite defeat on that opening day against Chelsea, García scored. A superb goal followed against AFC Wimbledon in the Carabao Cup. “It was super special to do it at Craven Cottage. I love how close the fans are – they can reach out and touch you. But I don’t consider myself someone who’s easily satisfied. I’m not like that. I always want more, more, more.”

García hasn’t scored since and Fulham went five league games without a win, pressure building. Which is where the calmness comes in. By the time they faced Hull, Arbeloa appeared on the edge of the sack, questions asked about his signings, García especially. Were three Madrid academy kids really what Fulham needed? Was the coach’s relationship with them not such a good thing after all?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

No player is impermeable to what is said, García admits, but he insists: “We treat that as outside noise. And we all knew that the beginning wouldn’t be easy. There’s a change of cycle: the coach goes, a new coach comes, there are signings, a different system, idea. Everyone has to adapt: those already at the club and those of us who are new. We’re young too. Results weren’t going our way but we had good intentions: to play good football, build, apply the manager’s ideas bit by bit. We had to remain calm.”

Fulham go into Saturday’s game at Manchester City unbeaten in four in the league, the sense of them shifting towards something more pragmatic not shared by García. “I don’t think we changed anything against Hull,” he says of a game Fulham won 1-0. “We didn’t do anything we weren’t already doing. Nothing. Maybe we controlled the small details that hurt us but the idea was the same. The players were very clear what the manager asked, very firm: it was just a question of time. You have to be patient. If you watch Fulham, you see the manager’s idea: have the ball, construct attacks well, show maximum intensity constantly with and without the ball. Aggressive, ambitious.”

Chances are coming for García but goals aren’t. He has started every league game but not scored or assisted since the opening day. Yet if there is a sense of a man feeling the pressure, that’s not repeated here; instead there’s an evenness, an ease. And a smile when another, more welcome, stat is raised: he has made more off‑the‑ball runs into the area than anyone. Something to hold on to, perhaps, a process that will pay off. “Really?” he says. “Well, I’m happy for people to see that a striker can help the team without the ball. In the end, it’s about following the manager’s instructions.”

In the end, though, teams will be judged on results and strikers on goals, price too. He knows: this is what he does, the path he chose. “Pressure depends on how you look at it, really,” García says. “Football is [very psychological]. It happens fast: it doesn’t give you time to enjoy good moments or linger on bad ones. It’s a rollercoaster – up there, down here. It’s not flat, but you maintain balance, work daily, improve: go in, focus, repeat.

“It’s not that I don’t ‘care’ about the price, it’s that the market is the market; it doesn’t depend on me. Calmness always, perspective … I know strikers are measured by goals but, well, the days I don’t score I’m completely sure I will be able to walk off the pitch and say that, no matter what happened, I helped my team, doing a load of other things. It is what it is.”

It is also time. A head peers around the door, the bus is going. García holds out a hand, apologises again. “It’s been a pleasure,” he says.

#882. Rochdale sack boss Watson after Northampton defeat

Ian Watson was in his first EFL managerial role at Rochdale

Rochdale have sacked head coach Ian Watson after only five months in charge of the League Two club.

The former South Shields boss replaced promotion-winning manager Jimmy McNulty in June after he joined Stockport but leaves the club just two points clear of the relegation zone.

Watson took South Shields to the National League North play-off final last season where they were beaten by Kidderminster Harriers before taking up his first Football League role at Spotland.

After returning to the EFL by beating Boreham Wood in last season's National League promotion final, Rochdale have won only four of their 16 League Two matches so far this season.

He departs following Saturday's 3-2 defeat by Northampton Town which was their fourth successive loss and left them 22nd in the table.

"We would like to thank Ian for his hard work and commitment during his time at the Crown Oil Arena and wish him every success in the future," said a club statement., external

"The process to appoint a successor is already underway, and the club will give a further update in due course."

Rochdale are next in action at home to Barnet on Saturday, 28 November (15:00 GMT).

#881. Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet

The 30-year-old former England star combines Twitch streaming with working to return to the top as a player

Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.

“We’ll do maybe two days on, one day off, and then three days on, one day off,” says Peters. “We’ve been doing that for just over a year now. It’s full-on. It’s pretty much as if you were at a club.”

Dele rose as a teenager to a level of stardom few experience and, used to media attention, doesn’t mind that his absence from football draws scrutiny. But he disagrees with the suggestion that choosing to stream on Twitch is a sign he has lost interest in the game that made him wealthy enough to never need to work again.

To a modest Twitch audience, he sometimes plays video games, sometimes just talks. He has a knack for creating viral content, sharing a phone call with Harry Kane and playing a game of EA Sports FC with IShowSpeed, one of the most famous online influencers. When he lost that game – and a bet – he wore an Arsenal shirt, apologising to Spurs fans before burning it. When TalkSport pundits claimed Dele was wasting his potential by becoming a streamer, Dele responded in a live stream, pointing out he was recording himself in his spare time and if he was out at nightclubs, it would be worse. Even then he was polite.

“When people see him online streaming or whatever he does in his private time, the initial thought is: ‘He’s done with football, then,’” Peters says. “He’s been training for a year and a half by himself. If he was done with football he wouldn’t be doing that. His actions show that the hunger is still there. A lot of people would come out of the game and then stop and lose the hunger for it, but he’s still chipping away every day, trying to get back and get to somewhere that he’s happy with.”

Dele broke through at MK Dons as a slight but devilish defensive midfielder, dominating League One midfields full of hardened professionals, before being scouted by Tottenham. Mauricio Pochettino attended MK Dons’ 4-0 League Cup win against Manchester United in 2014 and saw enough to leave early and convince Daniel Levy to pay £5m.

By the time Dele turned 21, his statistics were superior to Cristiano Ronaldo’s at the same age: 26 goals and 14 assists to Ronaldo’s 14 and 13. His 40 goal involvements equalled Frank Lampard, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham combined at the same age.

“He’s scored more in his first 50 league games than Steven Gerrard, Wayne Rooney and Frank Lampard,” Pochettino wrote in his book Brave New World. “He may go on to be better than all of them because he has the quality; now he just needs consistency.”

But there were, perhaps, warning signs of what would happen at Spurs. One source who worked closely with Dele describes him as a “cheeky chappy”; charming and universally popular.

He wasn’t one to miss training, but there were concerns he wasn’t leading the pristine lifestyle of many elite players, and tabloid stories about his private life trailed him. Pochettino was concerned when he saw Dele’s WhatsApp photo, a cartoon of a boy surrounded by people wanting a piece of him, believing he needed support from the right people. John McDermott, the head of coaching and development, said: “When the trough is full, the pigs come from all over to feed.”

When Dele voluntarily liquidated one of his companies this month, documents showed an estimated surplus after costs of £7.6m, suggesting the 30-year-old has not squandered the millions he earned at his peak in wages and sponsorship agreements, including a five-year deal with Adidas. He also owns a property portfolio worth more than £1.5m.

In the early days Pochettino warned Dele about the danger of not giving maximum effort in matches and training, a sentiment later shared by José Mourinho when he became Spurs manager. “I think one day you will regret, if you don’t reach what you can reach,” Mourinho told Dele in his office as Amazon Prime’s cameras rolled.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although Dele formed a formidable relationship with Kane on the pitch, and was twice named the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s young player of the year while playing behind the striker, he was closer to Eric Dier off it. And perhaps it was those anchors – Pochettino and Dier – that Dele lost later in his career.

His time with Pochettino was fondly remembered. For the Argentinian’s 50th birthday celebrations, Dele recorded a heartfelt video for his former manager. “The message was beautiful,” says one party-goer.

In almost five years since leaving Spurs, he has made one league start at Everton and 10 at Besiktas, before a loan at Como, where Cesc Fàbregas tried to rediscover the player he once was. He came off the bench once and was sent off nine minutes later.

Dele, according to those close to him, is biding his time to get his next move right. He will be 31 in April and wants a suitable contract. He has spoken to a host of clubs, with interest from the Premier League and the Championship, and from the Middle East, where he has been tempted by the riches of the Saudi Pro League, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. There has also been interest from Major League Soccer and he has held talks with clubs in Brazil and Japan. It is believed he will join a club this season.

In preparation, Peters is also guiding Dele’s nutrition, though he does not require much guidance. “Del’s a weird one, because he doesn’t snack, he doesn’t eat unhealthily, he doesn’t have a Sprite or a Coke or whatever. He’s never really been that kind of guy. All he does is drink coconut water, and he’ll have a small lunch, or his cheat day will be a Nando’s or something.”

Happiness is his priority. He spoke candidly on Gary Neville’s The Overlap in 2023 about his struggles with mental health and an addiction to sleeping pills after revealing abuse as a child. “Because he’s had such a long time out, he’s like: ‘What’s another few months if it means that I’m going to find something I’m actually happy with?’” Peters says. The aim is to “carry on for as long as possible”.

For the time being, Dele’s days are simple. When not training, he goes for coffee or a swim, and he has taken up padel. “He’s very much a person that’s happy with the little things,” Peters says. “He’s always the person that’s positive, the one that, if the group’s down or whatever, is going to pick everyone up. He’s happy with what he’s doing. His main happiness is playing football, and that’s what he wants to do.”

#880. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

#879. 'Officials can't use common sense' - was Rogers handball correct?

Leeds dominate Chelsea for first Stamford Bridge win since 1999

It is rare when a key handball decision is given for the widespread response to be "that is correct".

Often the discussion centres on the desire for a seemingly more lenient interpretation taking into account perceived intent.

And that is again a talking point after the crucial penalty given against Chelsea in Saturday's 4-1 home defeat by Leeds which ended up putting the visitors ahead for the first time.

Interestingly, despite the perception, handball penalties are much rarer in the Premier League compared with the other top five leagues in Europe.

Last season, there were 22 penalties for handball in the English top flight's 380 games - easily the lowest tally.

Spain's La Liga (36) and Italy's Serie A (38) produced the most.

This season in the Premier League there have been three in 106 matches - less than in 2025-26.

So why was the penalty given against Chelsea's Morgan Rogers?

'Fragile' and 'miles off it' - Alonso's Chelsea honeymoon is over

The feeling among Premier League clubs is that handball is in a good place now, where the arm must either be fully extended away from the body, raised, or be a deliberate act to be punishable.

And it is the last of these that applied to the penalty given against Rogers, which to some might seem a bit harsh, considering the Premier League's more relaxed interpretation of handball.

There are, however, a few key reasons why referee Michael Oliver pointed to the spot, why the video assistant referee (VAR) did not intervene, and why it will be judged as a correct decision.

Two of the factors which a referee looks for when judging a potential handball apply here.

As Jayden Bogle's shot was from distance, a defender is considered to have more time to adjust their body and react - and thus avoid a potential handball.

Most important in this case is the movement of the arm.

When Bogle shoots, Rogers' arm is not raised - but it comes up to the flight of the ball.

Crucially, had Rogers kept his arm in its original position - lower and level with his midriff - there would not have been a handball offence.

What does this mean? Put simply, if the ball would have hit the body if it had not come off the arm, it is considered to have no impact.

But this case was different. Rogers raised his arm and that is what led to the ball being deflected away. This is considered a deliberate act, and this trumps all other considerations.

I wish Oliver had the opportunity to see handball again - Hart

Perhaps there was a question about whether the ball hit Rogers too high on his arm, and thus should not be a handball offence.

It was close, but it looked like it was in what the laws call the 'red zone', the part of the arm which is punishable for handball.

But this really would be the only reason the VAR, Michael Salisbury, would have any cause to consider an on-field review.

We saw a similar case last season, in terms of how this kind of handball offence is judged - coincidentally involving a penalty awarded to Leeds.

As Anton Stach's powerful strike arrowed towards goal, Everton defender James Tarkowski leaned to his left in an attempt to block the shot - and did so with his arm, which was tucked tightly to the side of his body.

Everton manager David Moyes described the decision as "wrong", but it was absolutely correct in law.

That Tarkowski's arm was close to his side was irrelevant because of the deliberate act of leaning into the path of the ball.

Likewise, Rogers raised his arm to stop the ball and a penalty was a justifiable call.

Despite the Premier League having a more lenient interpretation of the handball law already, it is clear that many observers would like it to go further.

For example, BBC Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer echoed many when he said there should be more intent for a handball.

"I didn't agree with the penalty when Michael Oliver gave it," he said.

"I know once the on-field decision is made there is a high bar to review it, but I don't think officials are allowed to use common sense.

"Morgan Rogers is not deliberately trying to stop the ball. He just doesn't want it hitting him in the face.

"Although the penalty came at an important point in the match, Chelsea were deservedly beaten by a much stronger, far more physical and better-organised Leeds team."

Rogers may argue he raised his arm to protect his face.

This is one of the possible mitigating factors, but usually only applies when a player raises their hands to their face - not using the arm as a barrier.

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso said that, while he did not "want to make a big thing about it", the penalty should not have been awarded.

"For me it was quite a harsh decision," he told Sky Sports. "I would not have given a penalty. I don't want to make a big thing about it but for me it's not a penalty."

#877. How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he says.

At the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

His experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The company advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

Much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she says.

Although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” says Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Looking back, Asare says that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire.

Impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, says Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers

Much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” says Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, says Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

If impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper issue or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, says Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, says Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something big, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

#876. César Azpilicueta: ‘At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe – if you can’t perform, you’re out’

Former defender reflects on his record-breaking longevity, kicking Eden Hazard in training, and life after retirement

César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot.

It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. Now, at 37, it’s not the same, although there remains much to do, Azpilicueta as understated and quietly busy as ever: “square,” he calls himself. He’s completed an MBA, a sports directorship diploma and there are media offers, a life to live. Matches to play still: against his kids the needle is never far away, he says. And although he hasn’t found a seven-a-side team yet he will.

“I get up, take them to school, go to the gym. I do pilates some days. I walk the dogs, play golf, then it’s after-school activities. I read, try to learn new things. I haven’t yet thought: ‘I’m bored,’” Azpilicueta says, although you wonder how long that will last. “Over the last 12 months I could see it. The summer before I already ‘hit the post’ with retirement. It’s natural: a day comes … if only I could play for ever but it is what it is and you have to keep evolving. I’m enjoying it.”

Don’t get the wrong idea. “In terms of controlling your time, playing every three days, always waiting on the next message: ‘Meet at …,’ it’s a release. But it’s not a liberation because you’re delighted to pull your boots on. An important part of your life ends; you kick a ball almost from the moment you walk, live your passion. Even last season – when there were days everything hurt, when you think: ‘How can I get injured like that?’

– I would make demands of myself, my teammates. I always liked that.

“I never thought I’d be a professional. I couldn’t tell you the moment I thought: ‘I’m a footballer,’” Azpilicueta says, but he can tell you the score on his debut, for Osasuna in 2007. “One-nil win, Getafe.” Celta Vigo were the last opponents: a 1-0 loss in May for Sevilla. Between those, more than 800 matches, 508 for Chelsea. Only five players have played more for Chelsea; no foreigner has.

“I don’t think anyone who saw me back then could explain how I played 11 years at Chelsea … and nor could I,” Azpilicueta says, and there’s that laugh again. It’s a long time since he stood before his new teammates and sang an Estopa track. He arrived in London with a labrador and a sausage dog; he left a legend and the captain, with three kids and every trophy, a European and world champion.

Asked to define his career in a word, Azpilicueta goes for: constancia. Perseverance, consistency, commitment. He talks about the cruciate tear with Marseille aged 21 as a lesson, something that “changed my perspective and made me value discipline, preparation … Out of something negative I grew.” About always adapting, always overcoming, becoming what managers need you to be. There’s a laugh at the little lies – of course I’ve played on the left, boss – and the hours spent alone practising, convincing coaches or teammates to stay behind with him and go over it again and again.

“I arrived at Chelsea late in the market [in 2012],” Azpilicueta says. “My representative said: ‘We’ve spoken to Michael Emenalo, the sporting director, and they’re signing younger players.’ Oscar, Eden Hazard, Victor Moses, Marko Marin, Paulo Ferreira. I was 22. Doubts? Pfff … Olympique needed the money. Chelsea had just won the Champions League and I …”

That laugh. “I hadn’t played for Spain. What did Emenalo see in me? It’s hard to work it out. Also, what you are and what you become is different. You think: ‘What’s it going to be like?’ Another country, another pace, but Juan Mata was there, Fernando Torres, Oriol [Romeu]. Dr [Paco] Biosca, Ivan the physio. Petr Cech spoke Spanish. Hazard and I spoke French together. I could [communicate] with the Brazilians. But it wasn’t just them. I integrated fast, tried to speak English.

“Not long after arriving there was this audience with fans. Fernando, Juan, Oriol and I. A Q&A. One said: ‘Look, your name is very difficult. Can we just call you Dave?’ Juan translated. I said: ‘Yeah, sure,’ thinking that they meant for the evening. And it stuck. Going down the street: ‘Hey, Dave!’ There was the occasional ‘Dave’ in the dressing room but mostly it was fans. I felt the affection.

“You go with an open mind and bit by bit carve yourself a place. Every time a new coach comes you think: ‘Now what? Will I fit?’ I started as a winger in Pamplona. At Chelsea I played right-back, left-back, a line of three which I hadn’t played in my life … lots of systems, lots of coaches.”

Twelve coaches, in fact. Azpilicueta played under all of them. “You arrive at a historic club like Chelsea and just try to stay as long as you can. That machine makes demands of you every three days. What I really noticed was a hunger to win: either you have that culture or … forget it. At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe. You see teammates come and go. The reality is the reality. On the pitch, you have to do it. It’s hard? Yes. But you can’t be sunk by a bad game. If you win: very good, done, next. If you can’t perform, you’re out … You have to manage that pressure.

“I’ve had plenty of unpleasant days. I remember a 6-0 loss to Manchester City.” So then what? “For me, the first thing would be watch the video. Look at the data. But know that’s not everything. Sleep, get up, turn it round. Get into training first. And it’s not just about you; some days it’s about lifting up teammates too.”

Preparation, he says, was fundamental. “I analysed everything. I want to know if when the winger receives, he turns left. I needed that. Football’s not mathematical – ‘this equals that’ – but that information helps you have more control, feel readier. I don’t know if I was more [serious] than others, but I was very cuadriculado, square. Others hardly did anything and were fine.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

That sounds like Hazard. Azpilicueta laughs. “He was more … more … relaxed. Not everyone has to be the same. I was very square, I prepared differently, I was like a robot.”

Besides, Hazard was the best; it is his name, not Lionel Messi or Ronaldo’s, that comes up when Azpilicueta is asked his toughest opponent. “I was fortunate to train with Eden. He didn’t train 100%, but he forced you to. I had to kick him sometimes, haha! Playing together, he would say: ‘Give me the ball.’ I would say: ‘Stay there, I’ll defend for you.’”

Azpilicueta defended them all. “The first time I was captain was an FA Cup semi-final against Tottenham [in 2017],” he says. “We arrived late, no one said anything. [Gary] Cahill, the captain, was injured. We walk in and, pam, the armband’s in my place. Steve Holland says: ‘Let’s go to the referees meeting.’ ‘Oh, OK’ … and that was it. I liked it. I don’t think you change much; you have your own personality. You don’t have to score two because you’re captain. Besides, that was a one-off until later. But you do feel a little extra responsibility.”

New players found Azpilicueta waiting for them, leadership through empathy and example. “Quite a few stayed at my house,” he says. But if there is a portrait of his leadership perhaps it is him paying for the bus, covering petrol for the first team and youth team, when Chelsea’s assets were frozen after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. And his reaction to that being put to him now. “Nah,” he says. “Well. No. All of us. I didn’t do anything anyone else didn’t. We did it together, which is how things should be done.

“There a feeling of: ‘We have this issue, we’re going to sort this out,’” Azpilicueta says, fist hitting the desk. “That situation was strange. We had won the Club World Cup, been with [Roman Abramovich] there and suddenly … it was the uncertainty: players, staff. Many people work for Chelsea, depend on that.”

Underlying it all is the same basic principle, Azpilicueta says: “People. There are so many day-to-day who make it work. And sure, we’re good at football but what really fulfils you is see people there with their families all together when you win, when you lift the Champions League.”

Have you got a photo of you lifting that cup? “At home? No. A friend gave me a very nice one framed but it’s half hidden. I don’t much like showing it off.” If someone came to your house could they tell a footballer lives there? “No.”

Twenty years on, a lifetime later, a footballer doesn’t. So now what? “I don’t know,” Azpilicueta says, laughing. “Maybe I’ll be here, playing off a better handicap. But I like football, being involved. I’ve done some co-commentating. I have the MBA, the diploma. Not because I necessarily want to be a sporting director tomorrow, but because it interests me, because it’s nice to learn. I enjoyed the classes, meeting people, doing course work.”

The practical experience is even better. “The last few contracts I negotiated myself. I’ve had various agents help over the years but a time came with Chelsea when I thought: ‘What for?’ I sit down with Marina [Granovskaia], then with Behdad [Eghbali] and Todd [Boehly]. As captain I had spoken to them about so many issues that when it came to my own I thought: ‘I can do this alone.’ I might have got a better deal, who knows, but I was comfortable that way. I was never looking for anything, I was happy, my family was happy, I felt loved and valued and that was it. I just wanted to go in to work every day.”
