#797. From conceding seven to Hull heroics - how Tzolakis recovered to defy Brighton

McBurnie stoppage-time double earns Hull win over 10-man Brighton

Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic used one word to describe the performance of his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis in Sunday's 2-0 Premier League win against Brighton.

"Unbelievable," he told Match of the Day.

"Especially after the international break, which was very difficult for him."

Tzolakis' previous outing had been for Greece against the Netherlands in the Uefa Nations League, where he and his side were humbled 7-0 by the hosts in Amsterdam.

Nine days later, his contribution to the Tigers' first league victory since 29 August was every bit as important as that of striker Oli McBurnie, who netted both goals in second-half stoppage time against the second-placed Seagulls.

Tzolakis made a series of top saves to keep the highest scorers in the top flight at bay and, when Brighton full-back Costinha was sent off in the 89th minute for a second bookable offence, the hosts seized their opportunity to clinch only their third win following their Premier League return.

McBurnie said the 24-year-old stopper had "kept Hull in a few games" this season and the club were "lucky to have him", while Tzolakis told Sky Sports: "We are a unit and a team.

"We play for each other. We showed a good team effort and we deserved the three points."

McBurnie scores stoppage-time double as Hull stun Brighton

How 'outstanding' Tzolakis kept Brighton at bay

With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just could not find a way past former Olympiacos goalkeeper Tzolakis, who joined Hull in August for a reported Â£20m fee.

He got down to make a vital block early on to deny Diego Gomez, who had slid in to meet a low cross from the left wing. It was the first of several occasions the Paraguay international would be frustrated in front of goal.

Tzolakis then raced out spreadeagled to foil Georginio Rutter with an outstretched left hand - a stop that BBC Radio 5 Live pundit and former striker Clinton Morrison described as "Peter Schmeichel-esque", referring to the legendary Denmark keeper.

Second-half efforts from distance by Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk were dealt with, too.

Yasin Ayari went close with a thumping strike against the bar and when Brighton substitute Charalampos Kostoulas pounced on a short backpass to go through one-on-one, Tzolakis got a hand on his Greece team-mate's shot and Regan Slater was back on the goalline to head the ball to safety.

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy, a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said: "We saw again how important Tzolakis is for Hull. He had one of those days where he was always in the right place at the right time.

"When you are a Hull player and you see the kind of saves Tzolakis made when he spread himself and kept it out with his foot, you start thinking that it could be your day.

"It happens a lot in football and, on the flip side, Brighton will have been thinking, 'are we ever going to score here?'."

Hull made a superb start to the campaign after being promoted via the Championship play-offs in May.

They followed victories against Manchester United and Coventry with a draw against Aston Villa - all without conceding a goal.

The Tigers had not won since that 1-0 success at Coventry until beating Brighton - but they are one of four top-flight sides still unbeaten at home and have not lost any fixture by more than a one-goal margin.

They lost 1-0 to champions Arsenal before the international break and Scotland forward McBurnie told Match of the Day: "We know we can make it difficult for the top teams in the league and we've proved that in the past two games.

"We want to make it as difficult as we can for teams to come here and make the MKM Stadium a tough place to come. It's proving that way so far, so long may it continue."

#796. Miley Cyrus’ Wedding Dress Revealed: Details on Her Backless Gown

Miley Cyrus wore a stunning long-sleeved gown for her and Maxx Morando’s Palm Springs wedding, where she said "I do" in front of mom Tish Cyrus, dad Billy Ray Cyrus and more.

Miley Cyrus’ wedding dress is one in a million.

The Hannah Montana alum tied the knot with Maxx Morando in Palm Springs, Calif., Nov. 21 after five years of dating. And while the ceremony was an emotional affair for everyone in attendance, it was Miley’s dress that stole the show like a wrecking ball.

The 33-year-old was a vision in white as she donned a long-sleeved, backless gown designed by Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello to exchange vows with Maxx, according to photos of the newlyweds, shot by photographer Jose Villa, which Miley shared on Instagram Nov. 22.

To really allow the most-wanted gown to shine, the 33-year-old wore her hair in a tousled up-do.

And it’s clear the nuptials were something beautiful as photos from the ceremony showed Miley wiping away tears as she stood in front of the Liily drummer, per photos obtained by DeuxMoi.

As for the loved ones who watched their butterflies fly away to a new chapter, Miley’s mom Tish Cyrus and stepdad Dominic Purcell were just two family members who witnessed Miley and Maxx throw down their vows.

Additionally, her sisters Brandi Cyrus and Noah Cyrus watched on as the “Flowers” singer proved her heart beats for love. Plus, Miley’s father Billy Ray Cyrus and his partner Elizabeth Hurley did the same alongside Elizabeth's son Damien Hurley.

One night before the ceremony, Miley’s stepsister Lily-Rose Purcell shared special details from the couple’s rehearsal dinner Nov. 20.

In fact, she shared a close-up of the event’s dinner menu on Instagram Stories, which included a main course of filet mignon and Maine lobster ravioli, followed by a dessert selection of chocolate caramel layer cake, vanilla crème brûlée and raspberry sorbet.

But the breakout detail had to be the “M+M” printed at the top of the menu—a nod to the couple’s first initials.

Maxx, 28, and Miley began dating in 2021 after a mutual friend set them up on a blind date. Four years later, the pair confirmed their engagement in December 2025 after the “Toro” musician popped the question during a vacation in Japan.

"I’m not totally the boss in our house," Miley told Zane Lowe in an interview shared by Apple Music Sept. 17. "It's like a sense of relief that I can actually soften into, because he’s going to watch this and be like, 'You’re not the boss. We’re both the boss.'"

And it’s that playful banter that she’s especially excited to bring into their marriage.

As she put it, "I think that’s the thing that maybe generations prior didn’t teach us, that marriage doesn’t need to be a prison. It can actually be a playground."

Keep reading for a closer look into Miley and Maxx’s love story…

Miley Cyrus and musician Maxx Morando began dating in 2021. "We got put on a blind date," she recalled to British Vogue in 2023. "Well, it was blind for me and not really for him. I thought, 'The worst that can happen is I leave.'"

Miley didn't leave and, as their romance blossomed, the pair went red carpet official at the Gucci Love Parade event on November 2, 2021.

Miley and Maxx, who is a drummer in the band Liily, enjoyed a night out seeing Chicago on Broadway.

The "Flowers" singer and her boyfriend stepped out together at a Versace runway show in West Hollywood on March 9, 2023.

Maxx was by Miley's side when she won her first-ever Grammy at the 2024 award ceremony. The couple even shared a sweet smooch at their table during the event, and Miley referred to Maxx in her acceptance speech as "my love."

They returned to the Grammy Awards in 2025 for another public date night. "He’s very similar to me," Miley told Harper's Bazaar in an interview published November 2024. "We just don’t take life too seriously."

Maxx, who is six years younger than the Hannah Montana star, joined Miley on the red carpet at SNL50: The Anniversary Special, to celebrate 50 years of Saturday Night Live.

The musicians got glammed up for a big night out at the 2025 Oscars ceremony.

And later that night they stepped out in fresh looks for an appearance at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party.

It was a party in the U.S.A. when the pair got married in Plam Springs.

#795. 'A shotgun marriage': Why are NASA's SkyFall Mars helicopters riding on a nuclear rocket?

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

"The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket.

NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet.

But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the "Mars Czar") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'"

Hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform.

Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management issues." Since the SkyFall mission concept first appeared, he said, the usual sequence for a science mission is reversed.

"The science community is having to scramble to back into a set of requirements and objectives that match the SkyFall capabilities. Fortunately the community is very creative," said Hubbard, "and the basic Planetary Decadal objectives are very broad."

Decadal surveys reflect a broad consensus within the scientific community and provide detailed insights into the strategic priorities and mission directives set for the next decade across key scientific domains, including planetary exploration.

However, Hubbard said he has heard griping about the "fait accompli" process, "but the planetary community will make lemonade."

It should be noted however, Hubbard continued, that this process is not how you would design a strategic set of missions as precursors for human exploration.

"SR-1 Freedom is a technology demo that may or may not be ready for the Mars launch window in 2028. It is clear that the Mars Program has a standard launch concept in their back pocket," said Hubbard. "Nuclear Electric Propulsion [NEP] is of little value in traveling to Mars, not shaving any time off the transit. The real value of NEP is for risk reduction, use at the moon, outer planets and even bolder ideas like interstellar travel," Hubbard concluded.

"This, by far, is the shortest Mars mission ever conceived of," said Matthew Golombek, SkyFall Project Scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., speaking Nov. 10 during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

Kick-started by NASA in March 2026, the SkyFall project has grown from roughly six people to over 200 individuals who are now working on the initiative, said Golombek. "This is an incredibly rapid development and build," he said.

"It's really to demonstrate that exploration is possible with helicopters … filling what I call a 'resolution gap' between orbital information and surface information," Golombek told the MEPAG.

Once deployed by a helicopter deployment system, the threesome will spin up their rotors at about a kilometer above the surface of Mars. Then each helicopter lands on its own, ready to undertake flights every other solar day on the Red Planet. On average, a day (labeled as a sol) on Mars lasts 24 hours 39 minutes 35 seconds, from one noon to the next.

SkyFall's prime mission is six months, with a one-year goal," Golombek said, and the intent is to arrive in northern spring on Mars, a time where the vehicles are unlikely to encounter dust storms.

On the to-do list of NASA level one science requisites are for the helicopters to capture high-resolution imagery, perform a set scientific tasks, and help to prepare for future human exploration of Mars, said Golombek.

From their initial landing spots, the whirlybirds could potentially go tens to 100's of kilometers or more in different directions. Identical for all three helicopters, the nominal payload consists of five instruments, plus engineering navigation cameras.

That gear can examine the subsurface structure of Mars, the geomorphology and geology of surface terrains, as well as look at the meteorology of the atmosphere and the planet's radiation environment.

"The real star of the show is ground penetrating radar [GPR] with a flexible antenna," Golombek noted. That ultra-small GPR hardware can look for buried rocks, the layering of the Mars home turf, as well as spot subsurface ice deposits.

"If you have this aerial access and the ability to scout ahead," Golombek said, "you would go a long way towards better defining where to go with a rover and what kind of more detailed surface studies to do with subsequent missions."

All that said, yet to be plotted out are science-focused traverses for the SkyFall helicopters. But there are early ideas.

"The real kicker is that these spacecraft are the smallest landers ever attempted on Mars," said Golombek. "You are looking for a place that virtually has no rocks," he pointed out, a must-have to assure high probability of landing safely. So toss in for good measure low surface slopes, no big craters, a site not overloaded with dust.

One early idea is to revisit the crash locales of discarded SkyFall descent hardware – fuel tanks, cruise stage and associated gear – equipment large and heavy enough to survive entry, smack into the Mars landscape and high-speed and generate craters.

"So if there is ice at centimeters depth, we would create our own icy impact craters," Golombek said. "We could actually visit them in a time-scale before the ice actually sublimates," he said.

Another site getting the eye, albeit deemed a design reference target but considered a "pretty good spot," is within Arcadia Planitia in Mars's northern lowlands. Studies have indicated the presence of substantial volumes of near-surface excess ice there.

"There is a vast amount of information to suggest large quantities of regional ice deposits at that location," said Golombek. "This is at least one location that appears to meet all the engineering constraints and would be a potentially safe landing site…virtually no rocks," he advised.

In the past, Golombek added, JPL took part in SpaceX-sponsored workshops to look for ice deposits as close to the equator of Mars that could be found. Arcadia Planitia was flagged as superior Starship touchdown terrain.

"Most of the landing sites considered for humans have talked about going to places with ice deposits. Ice provides both a consumable as well as fuel to get back off the planet," said Golombek.

For the near-term, scientific community input next year — via two workshops — are on tap, reviewing the science of SkyFall and also help sort out potential landing sites for final decision-making at NASA Headquarters.

Meanwhile, as SkyFall literally spins up, there is the need for on-time delivery of Space Reactor-1 Freedom.

Golombek said NASA considers the two endeavors as a pair.

"If SR-1 is not ready, SkyFall could be launched on any conventional launch vehicle without any difficulty whatsoever," said Golombek, "something like a Falcon 9 would be more than sufficient, but others are possible as well."

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. #794. Fears of rising antisemitism in Europe

Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny commemorates the victims of Auschwitz as Jewish communities across Europe face growing hostility. What does the promise of "Never Again" mean for Jewish life in Europe today?

Regina Sluszny makes her way in her wheelchair through the iron gate marking the entrance to the former Auschwitz concentration camp. "I feel the cold, both physically and emotionally," says the 87-year-old Jewish woman, her gaze fixed on the grey horizon.

How many times has she been here? Six, seven, perhaps eight, she estimates. And each time, the same thoughts run through her mind: "I think about my husband's family. He lost seven loved ones here. They were sent straight to the gas chambers and murdered."

Regina Sluszny traveled to Poland with a delegation from the European Jewish Association (EJA), a European advocacy group representing Jewish interests that regularly organizes conferences on Jewish life as well as visits to former concentration camps.

This year, the organization invited political representatives and members of Jewish communities to Krakow and Auschwitz on November 9 and 10. The trip was deliberately scheduled to coincide with the anniversary of the November Pogroms of 1938, widely regarded as a watershed moment on the path to the Holocaust.

"Honoring the past, securing the future" is the event's motto. Like many others in attendance, Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny fears that the horrors of the Shoah are slowly fading from Europe's collective memory.

Among this year's international religious and political representatives, the guest of honor was Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah and a prominent opponent of the Islamic Republic. The European Jewish Association (EJA) honored him for his efforts to combat antisemitism.

Accepting the award, Pahlavi recalled the historic ties between the Persian and Jewish peoples and called on democratic nations around the world to unite against oppression and ideological extremism.

But talking to attendees at the symposium in Krakow, it quickly becomes clear that fear of rising antisemitism is much closer to home. Many describe growing hostility towards Jews and rising fear in Jewish communities across Europe.

In France, authorities recorded a total of 1,320 antisemitic incidents in 2025. That was fewer than in 2024, but around three times as many as in 2022.

In Germany, the number of antisemitic crimes recorded by police rose from 2,641 in 2022 to 6,236 in 2024 and 6,548 in 2025. Authorities and monitoring organizations across Europe have reported a significant increase in antisemitic incidents since October 7, 2023.

For Ellen van Praagh, chair of the Interprovincial Rabbinate in the Netherlands, October 7, 2023, marked a turning point. She also lost a family member during the Hamas-led attack which saw around 1,200 people in Israel killed and over 250 taken hostage and abducted to the Gaza Strip.

"My family has lived in the Netherlands since the 16th century. And now I'm being told to leave," says van Praagh. She says the atmosphere in the Netherlands has changed dramatically since the attack. She no longer feels safe there as a Jew. "We Jews are being held responsible for Israel's actions."

Israel launched a major military offensive in the Gaza Strip after the October-7 attack. More than 75,000 Palestinians have been killed there since the start of the war, according to conservative estimates.

Like many others at the symposium, van Praagh says she is increasingly losing faith in politicians. "Never Again" has become an empty phrase, she argues, with little relevance to the everyday lives of Jews in Europe.

Jewish communities now have to protect themselves behind high walls. Constant security measures restrict their daily lives, she explains. "That is not what we want. We want to live in freedom."

Rabbi Menachem Margolin, chairman of the European Jewish Association, is also calling on European political leaders to take greater responsibility. He says he is grateful for their support, without which Jewish life in Europe would hardly be possible.

However, laws designed to protect Jewish life are often not enforced in practice. Many officials hesitate to call antisemitism by its name as soon as doing so becomes politically inconvenient. "But Auschwitz did not begin with gas chambers. It began with words," he cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regina Sluszny joined the delegation visiting the Birkenau memorial. The Auschwitz concentration and extermination camp, built by Nazi Germany, became a symbol of the Holocaust. The Nazis murdered around 1.1 million people there, including approximately one million Jews. Most were killed here at Birkenau.

The delegation is gathered to commemorate the November Pogroms of November 9 and 10, 1938, when Nazis set synagogues on fire, ransacked Jewish businesses and homes and murdered Jews. Around 30,000 Jewish men were deported to concentration camps.

Survivors like Regina are increasingly rare. Most Holocaust survivors have passed away. Regina survived because, in 1942, a family friend and his wife took her in when she was just two years old while her parents fled the Nazis with her two brothers and went into hiding.

For more than 40 years, she has been sharing her story with schoolchildren, doing her part to ensure that the Holocaust is never forgotten. For her, "Never Again" is a promise that must be kept. Otherwise, it becomes a lie.

#793. The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.

It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two goals in quick succession.

Was there a case for the video assistant referee (VAR) to suggest it should be downgraded to a yellow?

Let's take a look at the incident, and what a referee takes into account before showing a red for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Ronald Araujo played a long ball upfield for Alexander Isak to run on to.

Isak took a touch, before Yoro bundled into the back of the Sweden international and brought him down.

Referee Sam Barrott did not hesitate, giving the foul and sending off Yoro.

Was there doubt that Isak would have taken control of the ball? If so, it should only be a caution.

There are four key considerations for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity:

distance between the offence and the goal

likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball

location and number of defenders and attackers

As Isak was running directly towards goal in a central position, and there was no covering defender, three of the factors were satisfied.

The question is about the "likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball".

The Liverpool striker took a heavy touch, which moved the ball a few yards ahead of him.

The touch came before contact from Yoro, so there is no case that the challenge caused Isak to over-run the ball.

The referee and the VAR, John Brooks, must therefore assess whether Isak would definitely have got to the ball ahead of Senne Lammens. And that if he had, it would have been a good scoring chance.

If there is any doubt, then it should not be a red card.

It is a borderline case, and as such the VAR would not be expected to intervene for a clear and obvious error.

Likewise, if the referee had shown a yellow the VAR would not get involved.

Former Liverpool and England midfielder Danny Murphy, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said there was "no doubt" about the red card.

Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville also agreed with the decision.

"Leny Yoro has to cover and he doesn't," Neville said on Sky Sports. "He reacts late and his anticipation is poor.

"It's so clumsy from Yoro. It's naivety, he just needs to get off the pitch. You're not going to get that turned around, no chance."

But for Liverpool boss Iraola the decision is not up for debate.

"I think he's the last man, no?" he said. "It's a clear foul and a red card, yes?

Did Liverpool 'get lucky' with red card decision?

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes felt it should not have been a red card and said the decision had a detrimental impact on the game.

"It's one that needs to be looked at," Fernandes told Sky Sports.

"We have far too many meetings with the referees for this to happen to us again. The last one against Chelsea [when Lisandro Martinez was sent off], you can give it as a red card and it was probably a second yellow also. Today, you can't give a red card.

"It's very clear they show us if the player is not in control of the ball, it's never a red card.

"Isak kicks the ball forward, the ball goes into the hands of Senne. Isak has got no control of the ball, he has no chance to get on the ball. He puts his leg across to try to get some advantage from Leny. I can understand the fall, but it's never a red card.

"There are too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR taking so long to see to make a mistake like this that can change the game.

"It's not because of them we conceded the goal from the free-kick, but it changes the game completely."

Pochettino, meanwhile, was frustrated by what he perceived as inconsistency in the decision-making of the officials.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss felt his new team should have been awarded a penalty moments before Yoro was sent off, after Jeremy Jacquet went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo.

"It's difficult to accept that because it was a foul under my view and for me was a penalty," Pochettino told Match of the Day.

"Look how everything changes if that action was a red card and a foul, I think we need to review. When I played football that situation is normal. The action against Mbeumo, if that [Yoro foul on Isak] was a red card then that was a penalty."

'We have too many referees' - Fernandes disagrees with Yoro red

There have been a couple of very similar cases this season.

Brighton's Pascal Struijk was sent off at Sunderland through a VAR review after he brought down Wilson Isidor.

The Seagulls successfully appealed against that red card on the grounds that there was clear doubt that Isidor would have taken control of the ball before it ran through to goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

Could Manchester United appeal against Yoro's red card? There's nothing to lose by doing so.

Despite the Football Association regulatory commission unanimously ruling the Struijk red card was wrong, the Premier League's key match incidents panel voted the VAR intervention was a correct call on a split 3-2 vote.

Ipswich's Issa Diop avoided a VAR red card for a foul on James McAtee against Nottingham Forest, when the referee disagreed with the video official, and believed there was a covering defender. Forest boss Oliver Glasner was adamant it had been a clear goalscoring opportunity.

It was the same referee, Thomas Bramall, for both of those incidents.

That shows just how subjective such decisions can be. It is often rare to get a real consensus.

Yoro can count himself a little unfortunate to get the red card.

Yoro sees red as Ngumoha shines - Liverpool v Man Utd player ratings

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

United Launch Alliance (ULA) is getting a handle on why its Vulcan Centaur rocket failed over the weekend.

That failure, which occurred during a launch from Florida's Space Coast on Sunday (Nov. 15), led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites. ULA soon traced the anomaly to Vulcan Centaur's first stage, and it has now pinpointed the problem area even further.

"While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines," ULA wrote in an update today (Nov. 18).

This is good news for Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos' aerospace company, which builds the BE-4. Two of these engines power Vulcan's first-stage booster, and they're also key to Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket: That heavy lifter features seven or nine BE-4s in its first stage, depending on the configuration. (New Glenn has its own issues at the moment; it exploded during a test on May 28, and Blue Origin is working to return the powerful rocket to flight.)

ULA had already said that Vulcan's six solid rocket boosters (SRBs) and its Centaur V upper stage — which employs a different engine, the RL-10 — seem to perform well on Sunday. Further analysis is firming up that conclusion, according to today's update.

Vulcan has had issues with its SRBs in the past. On the rocket's second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds into flight. On both occasions, Vulcan overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payload to orbit.

In the wake of the February flight, ULA and Northrop Grumman, which builds the SRBs, tweaked the nozzle design — a fix that apparently worked, based on Sunday's nominal performance.

Sunday's launch was the fifth ever for the two-stage Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has now experienced issues on three of its five flights, though Sunday's was the only one that ended in failure.

Vulcan was out of action for about nine months after the February SRB issue. It's unclear how long its current grounding will last; that depends on what ULA's anomaly investigation, which the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing, ends up finding.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #791. Tallulah Willis Regrets Sharing "Intimate" Photo of Dad Bruce Willis

Tallulah Willis detailed her regret over sharing a personal photo of her dad Bruce Willis as he continues to battle a form of dementia: "I can acknowledge that and vow to do better.”

Tallulah Willis is always in her father Bruce Willis’ corner.

One day after the 32-year-old shared a sweet father-daughter photo with The Sixth Sense star, who is currently battling a form of dementia, she explained why she ultimately felt it best to delete the snap.

“I posted a photo of my dad yesterday because we were having a BEAUTIFUL visit,” she wrote on Instagram Nov. 22 alongside a throwback photo with her dad. “I had someone take a super sweet photo of a shared moment between us watching a video of Frankie Valli singing.”

“I was very excited by the sweetness of the moment that I didn't think farther ahead that this was possibly too intimate a photo to show,” she added. “I can acknowledge that and vow to do better.”

In the now-deleted photo shared to her Instagram Nov. 21, Tallulah—who Bruce shares with ex-wife Demi Moore alongside daughters Rumer Willis, 38, and Scout Willis, 35—sat next to the 71-year-old on an outdoor porch swing as they held hands.

While Tallulah wore a red sweater, jeans and sunglasses as she wrapped one arm around the Die Hard star, he wore a gray cardigan and a pale pink shirt.

Though Tallulah decided it best to keep the memory between the pair of them, she acknowledged that she knows how much her updates mean to his fans.

“I know you all love him,” she added. “I love him. My family loves him. And he's still always the absolute hero we know him to be.”

She captioned the post, “I can do better.”

Bruce’s family shared he was diagnosed with FTD—an umbrella term for diseases that affect the frontal and temporal lobes of the brain, which are associated with personality and behavior, per Mayo Clinic—in 2023.

And recently, his wife Emma Heming Willis offered deeper insight into how the Willis family is coping with their new normal.

“It is extremely difficult and painful,” Emma—mom kids Mabel, 14, and Evelyn, 12, with Bruce—told Hello! In an interview published Sept. 7. “It's natural, we all want our loved ones to be healthy, full of life and being the person they always were. But FTD is a devastating illness that steals things from you very slowly. So the reality is that you find yourself constantly in a state of grief.”

But the dark chapter has been made brighter with the Willis women by her side.

“What has been truly beautiful to see throughout this process is how we all pour our hearts into supporting him—how deeply we love him, while completely respecting the way each person chooses to express that love,” she explained. “I think the balance we've found is simply a reflection of who Bruce is at his core; it’s the result of all the love and support he planted over the years coming right back to him now.”

#789. Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

The answer to one of Earth's greatest geological mysteries may lie deep beneath our feet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.

Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.

Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.

One of the most striking examples is found in the Grand Canyon, where rocks separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, as if some force or phenomenon removed the layers that geologists would expect to see in between. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity.

It's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana said in a statement.

"The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance."

In a new study published in the journal Nature, Dhungana and study co-author Nicolas Flament investigated whether activity far below Earth's surface was to blame.

Using computer models, they explored how the slow circulation of hot rock within Earth's mantle may have affected the continents over hundreds of millions of years.

The results suggest that three major ancient continental regions (Laurentia (modern North America), Baltica (northern Europe) and North China were gradually pushed up during the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately one billion to 540 million years ago. This would have left vast areas of land exposed to weathering and erosion for long periods, allowing water, wind and other processes to wear away rock that had formed much earlier.

But removing the rock is only part of the puzzle. They also needed to explain why the gaps are still visible today.

Their models suggest that the same regions subsequently began to sink. As sea levels rose relative to the land, sediment accumulated over the older, eroded surfaces, creating the sharp divide between ancient and younger rocks that we can still see today.

Crucially, the researchers found that the timing of the simulated continental uplift and sinking was consistent with geological evidence from North America, northern Europe and North China. This suggests that movements deep within Earth's mantle may have played a major role in shaping the geological record we see today.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#787. 90 Day Fiancé Alum Sheila Mangubat Dead at 35

90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days alum Sheila Mangubat has died at the age of 35, her former fiancé David Dangerfield confirmed: “I am devastated and still trying to process this loss.”

90 Day Fiancé fans are mourning a heartbreaking loss.

Sheila Mangubat—who appeared on 90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days in 2023—died in the Philippines on Nov. 21, her former fiancé David Dangerfield confirmed. She died just days before her 36th birthday, according to TMZ.

“It breaks my heart to share the news from her family that Sheila passed away on Saturday in the Philippines,” David wrote on Instagram Nov. 21 alongside a black-and-white photo of Sheila. “I am devastated and still trying to process this loss.”

“Please keep her son, her family, and me in your prayers,” the 45-year-old added. “Thank you for all your love and support.”

Sheila’s cause of death has not yet been confirmed.

As the reality star’s loved ones begin to grieve, her brother Jonathan Mangubat shared footage from Sheila’s funeral to his Facebook Stories Nov. 22, per TMZ, while her sister Grace Mangubat paid tribute to her late sibling on her own social media.

“Rest in peace my beloved sister,” she wrote on Facebook Nov. 21. “Sorry kaau layo kaau ko, dili ko kauli DHA.”

“Fly high my Sister,” she added. “We will miss you.”

Sheila and David’s romance was documented on season six of TLC’s 90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days in 2023. After meeting in a Facebook group for deaf singles in 2021, the pair sparked a long-distance romance, before becoming engaged. The former couple’s time on the show concluded with Sheila accepting David’s proposal.

In October 2025, Sheila and David broke up due to distance and K-1 visa issues, but rekindled their relationship in June, according to TMZ.

But David, who was born deaf, expressed that his love of Sheila—mom to son Jhonreil from a previous relationship—is eternal.

At the time, David saw forever in the TLC star.

“I will have a new family with Sheila in the future,” he vowed. “Sheila is better than any other woman I’ve dated because Sheila is a sweet person. She is the perfect match to me. I’ll love Sheila forever.”

#786. 'World's best could've lost 4-0' - but should Man Utd have done more at Anfield?

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino believes even the best team in the world could have conceded four goals at Liverpool in Manchester United's circumstances - but should the struggling Red Devils have done more in another disappointing defeat?

The former Tottenham and Chelsea manager's first match in charge of United got off to a dreadful start as they had defender Leny Yoro sent off in the eighth minute and were 2-0 down by the 13th minute.

That left them with a mountain to climb, with Liverpool scoring twice more in the second half to secure a 4-0 win that kept United second from bottom in the table.

"Do you think that is easy?" said Pochettino of the situation that faced his new side after those woeful opening 13 minutes.

"Even the best team in the world playing like this in this situation, in our circumstance, maybe concede the four goals or maybe more. And now what we are going to say?

"We are in a situation that this is very complicated. It's difficult, yes, but I think we fight, we made the effort, and I know how they feel now in the dressing room."

Mauricio Pochettino post-match interview - Liverpool v Man Utd

Trying to win any game when reduced to 10 men in the first half is difficult. In the entire history of the Premier League Manchester United have managed it on four occasions - each of those at Old Trafford.

Indeed, in the 509 instances of a team receiving one or more red cards in the first half of a Premier League match, they have gone on to win just 88 times.

At Anfield it gets even more difficult, with Arsenal the only team to have beaten Liverpool on their own ground after a first-half dismissal.

For ex-Manchester United captain Roy Keane, though, there are ways to lose if you have a man sent off - and a 4-0 defeat was not one of them.

Speaking before Pochettino's comments, he told Sky Sports: "Are you telling me they couldn't have done better? They lose 4-0 and everyone is saying it's not too bad.

"Has a team ever got a result before with 10 men? It can be done. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality. I can't believe what I'm hearing from people who have played for the club saying 4-0 is not too bad."

Keane was responding to his former team-mate Gary Neville, who was part of the commentary team for Sky Sports.

"That's where we've got to, where we're starting to write off 4-0 defeats at Anfield as though it's just the norm and what should be accepted," said Neville in the closing stages of the game. "The club's standards have dropped so far it's incredible."

The former England full-back added: "There'll be an element of, 'let's just forget about this game because Yoro got sent off, we've got 10 men and all that sort of stuff', but it rides into the game in midweek and from a defensive perspective I've never seen anything like this."

Keane did not agree with that view as he said: "Liverpool should have scored eight or nine. Unbelievable chances they had and everyone's coming off the pitch saying four is not too bad.

"I feel like swearing. I'll try not to. How can anyone say 4-0 is not too bad? Just because they went down to 10 men. That obviously made it a lot more difficult, but if you go down to 10 men is that it? Do you down tools and throw the towel in?"

Chaotic week, nightmare start and huge reality check for Pochettino

Pochettino endures nightmare start as Man Utd lose to Liverpool

The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

Despite Keane's comments, a 4-0 loss at Anfield isn't unthinkable - certainly better than losing 7-0 as United did three years ago.

But in the wider context it provides more concern about a defence that is now officially the worst in Europe's top five leagues.

No other team in the Premier League, La Liga, Bundesliga, Ligue 1 or Serie A has conceded more than United's 34 goals in all competitions so far this season.

It is also the second successive game they have conceded four goals, while in their last six games in all competitions they have conceded 19.

"I don't think Mauricio Pochettino can write this off," said ex-Leeds and Spurs goalkeeper Paul Robinson on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He has to learn from it. He will have learned about his players and their attitude.

"Liverpool had 27 shots in that game. There were mitigating circumstances early in the game... but why did we get to those circumstances?

"It was because defenders were out of position again. The long ball over the top that catches Matthijs de Ligt out, the lack of communication, the tackle Leny Yoro makes and the defenders being caught out."

#785. Legendary Jewelry Designer Paolo Bulgari Dead at 89

Paolo Bulgari—whose Bvlgari Group created unforgettable jewelry designs for stars like Elizabeth Taylor and Zendaya—has died at age 89.

Paolo Bulgari—famed jewelry designer and chairman of the Bvlgari Group—has died, the company confirmed on social media Nov. 21. He was 89.

“It is with deep sadness that we learned of the passing of Paolo Bulgari, grandson of the company’s founder Sotirio Bulgari and Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984,” the company said in a statement shared to Instagram. “Our deepest condolences go to his family, friends and all those who had the honor of sharing this journey with him.”

“Thank you, Mr. Paolo,” they added, “your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come.”

Born in Rome, Italy, in 1937, Bulgari—who shared four kids with ex-wife Alice Valli as well as two kids with wife Maite Caprio—was destined to carry on the family business from a young age.

“Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960,” the statement explained, “specializing in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world’s leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style.”

And it wasn’t long until he started making his own mark on the brand.

“A true creative soul, he poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers,” added the statement, “leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewelry.”

In fact, Bulgari, alongside his brothers Gianni Bulgari and Nicola Bulgari, played an integral role in shaping the brand’s distinctive style, becoming known for their use of bold shapes and standout gems.

They also expanded the business from jewelry into watches, perfumes and even hotels.

And over the decades, the brand’s creations have adorned stars from Elizabeth Taylor and Princess Diana to Zendaya and Anne Hathaway.

Just last month, Kim Kardashian said she might just “faint” in a video shared to Instagram Oct. 28 while getting a private tour of Taylor’s jewelry collection at the Bvlgari store in Italy, in which she was able to try on one of the late actress’ beloved pieces—an emerald and diamond necklace gifted to her by Richard Burton in 1962.

As Kardashian put it, “I am freaking out!”

And she of course had to thank her stylist Law Roach for making the dream come true, calling him on the phone to thank him for the “best” birthday present ever.

And while it’s true that Bulgari’s influence on fashion has stood the test of time, that’s because he believed “everything can be a source of inspiration.”

As he used to say, per Bvlgari’s statement, “There are no rules in creativity. Never.”

#784. A 'wow' player - why Ngumoha is already a Liverpool game-changer

Rio Ngumoha is going to be a 'wow' player for Liverpool - and he showed everyone exactly what he is already capable of in Sunday's 4-0 win over Manchester United.

He made an outstanding assist then added a fine finish, and there is much more to come. He plays without fear so he is going to score and make many more goals the same way.

Ngumoha has only just turned 18 but he is already a game-changer, someone who gets people excited because he is so hard to stop when he is one-on-one.

Of course he can frustrate you at times too, but that's what creative and explosive wingers like him do - and it's because he is so talented that everyone wants to see an end product from him every time he gets on the ball.

There were times against United when Ngumoha did not quite deliver, but he is still so young and I would much rather see players like him take too many touches - or try too many things and fail - than be afraid to try them in the first place.

So, if he runs out of play or runs into too many players at times, because teams are doubling up on him like United were, that just shows how scared they are of him.

His ability means he occupies opposition players - Youri Tielemans was always backing up Diogo Dalot on his wing to try to help him out, but that just meant United were leaving someone else free.

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Sometimes it is actually harder when you are playing out wide against 10 men because you don't get the same amount of space - United were not attacking the same way they would have done with 11, and they were sitting in more.

Yes, Ngumoha ran up the odd blind alley or got outnumbered but that is always going to happen. As he learns, and gets even better, his decision-making will improve too. He will know when to try to go past people or when to find that free man instead.

But he still showed all the bravery you want from a winger against United and, when you keep trying things the way he did, something is going to come off for you.

I look at Bradley Barcola in a similar way to Ngumoha - he can be frustrating but he tries things, and can be brilliant.

For Liverpool right now, one of the biggest positives is the competition they have in wide areas, with those two plus Victor Munoz and Cody Gakpo.

There are other areas of their squad, like left-back or central midfield, where that competition needs to improve, but I don't really worry about the wide attacking areas in the same way.

Sunday was only Ngumoha's second Premier League start of the season, and his first since the opening day.

He maybe only got his chance because Gakpo has a calf problem but, when everyone is fit, it is really exciting that they will all be thinking they have to play their best to push the manager and get in the team.

Andoni Iraola post-match interview - Liverpool v Man Utd

There were plenty of other positives for Liverpool, too. All in all, Sunday could not have gone much better for them.

United made a woeful start with poor concentration and mistakes which cost them but, from there, Liverpool saw the game out well.

Just because the opposition has a man sent off early on does not mean any kind of victory is a given, let alone a 4-0 win.

Look at how United's 11 men lost to City's 10 in the Manchester derby earlier this season - we've seen many times how good teams can frustrate a side with an extra player like that.

It definitely does not mean you are going to steamroller them, but Liverpool did that and made an abundance of chances to get even more goals.

Days like this are so important for building belief in all their attacking players, especially because they were playing at home, and against their big rivals.

Up until now, it had felt like Liverpool's better days this season had come on the road, but now the pressure and expectation is off them a bit - particularly if, like Ngumoha or Florian Wirtz, you have scored and played well.

I know from experience that, the next time they go back to Anfield, they will be buzzing. You know that the fans are already with you after you've scored against United, and you feel the love a little bit more.

This is the start of a big week for Liverpool and Iraola will probably make changes against Club Brugge in Belgium on Wednesday, knowing how difficult Sunday's Merseyside derby will be.

Everton is always a tough game but I think Liverpool will enjoy their trip to Hill Dickinson Stadium, and the confidence they will have after beating United will mean they can go there with a really positive mindset.

Danny Murphy was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

#783. Bundeswehr study exposes widespread sexual harassment in German military

Sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known, with younger women disproportionately affected. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has called for a policy of "zero tolerance."

"It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, on Wednesday.

Earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defense Committee. According to the findings, sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known.

"The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius said, announcing an action plan to address the issue.

"There is zero tolerance for sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr. This is nothing less than a matter of upholding the human dignity enshrined in our Basic Law. And that principle applies all the more within the Bundeswehr."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The study examined incidents that had gone unreported, the so-called "dark figure" of cases that never reach official statistics. The Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences (ZMSBw) surveyed 45,000 service members, around 18% of whom responded. More than 8,100 questionnaires were evaluated and supplemented with individual and group interviews. According to the institute, the data are statistically representative.

According to the study, younger women in the lower ranks are particularly affected by sexual misconduct. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. The perpetrators are predominantly male. Statistically, combat units do not differ from the rest of the armed forces.

Female service members in units with a higher proportion of women (more than 15%) are less likely to be affected.

Verbal harassment is by far the most common form of misconduct, according to the study. Around 72% of female soldiers and 31% of male soldiers said they had experienced verbal harassment at least once during their military service. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 38% of female soldiers and 16% of male soldiers reported experiencing verbal sexual harassment.

For physical harassment, 9% of female soldiers and 3% of male soldiers reported incidents of physical sexual misconduct, and 2% of both women and men said they had experienced sexual violence.

The study also examined why service members chose not to report incidents. The most commonly cited reason was not wanting to draw attention to themselves.

"There appears to be a lack of awareness of the reporting channels. And, for me, the decisive issue is trust in those channels," Pistorius concluded.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In response, the Bundeswehr plans to improve awareness of how and where cases of sexual harassment can be reported. That is precisely where the environmentalist Greens, who are in opposition in the Bundestag, direct their criticism.

Defense policy spokesperson Sara Nanni is calling for "an external reporting office, alongside the regular disciplinary process, with investigative powers and the authority to take disciplinary action where appropriate." Such an independent point of contact, she argues, is needed in cases where superiors within the Bundeswehr fail to fulfill their responsibilities.

Another consequence of the study is the expansion of support services for those affected. A counseling center established in early November will soon be available around the clock. Supervisors are also to receive enhanced awareness training and improved instruction.

"Sexual misconduct will become part of training at every level, from the very beginning," said Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer.

In addition, the way supervisors handle reported cases will become a standing criterion in their performance evaluations. "Anyone who fails to lead by example, tolerates misconduct, or does not address it consistently will no longer hold a leadership position," Defense Minister Pistorius stressed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The study was prompted by a growing number of reports of sexual misconduct received by former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces Eva Högl. Most of those who approached her were female soldiers. Högl called for the study into unreported cases in 2024. The process gained further momentum following incidents at the Parachute Regiment in Zweibrücken that came to light at the beginning of this year and also involved allegations of sexual misconduct.

The current Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, Henning Otte, described the figures revealed by the study as "dramatically high." The findings had also made it clear, he said, "that there is a lack of trust in the Bundeswehr's structures. The Ministry of Defense must now take this study seriously and translate its findings into a leadership culture that is truly lived in practice."

The Bundeswehr urgently needs additional personnel and has been actively recruiting women. However, the study's findings are unlikely to make attracting more female recruits any easier. Women remain significantly underrepresented across nearly all branches of the armed forces.

This article was originally written in German.

Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result. MAVEN launched to find out.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.

The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago.

MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars. The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result.

Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface, and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place.

NASA's MAVEN spacecraft was the first Mars orbiter ever built to measure how the Martian atmosphere interacts with solar wind, as well as how that constant stream of particles from the sun slowly stripped the Red Planet of its precious atmosphere over time.

After its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014. The spacecraft then spent the better part of 11 years studying the Red Planet from orbit using three different suites of instruments: An imaging ultraviolet spectrograph to study the global characteristics of the Martian atmosphere; a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectromenter to measure its composition; and a six-instrument setup to study how Mars' ionosphere reacts to solar wind.

"The science MAVEN has given us is key to informing what kind of radiation protection and safety measures we must take before sending humans to Mars," Louise Prockter, NASA director of planetary science, said in June 2026 after the mission concluded. "The data collected from MAVEN will continue to provide valuable insight into Mars for decades to come."

MAVEN was originally designed to study Mars for 1 full Earth year after arriving at the Red Planet. That mission ended in 2016, but the spacecraft managed to survive for another 10 years adding more observations for scientists to study.

NASA ultimately began using MAVEN as a communications relay for other missions at Mars as the orbiter aged. In December 2025, MAVEN went silent, with NASA losing communication with the orbiter.

An investigation later found that the probe sent its final signal on Dec. 6, 2025 as it was heading behind Mars (as seen from Earth). But when it emerged on the other side, it had gone into an uncontrollable spin that led to a loss of power, dooming the spacecraft.

NASA tried in vain to recover the spacecraft over several months, ultimately declaring the mission over in June 2026.

"Best. Mars. Mission. Ever," Shannon Curry, MAVEN's principal investigator, said of the probe's entire 12.5-year mission when it ended. The team "really experienced the loss of a loved one with the end of the mission here."

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#781. Chaotic week, nightmare start and huge reality check for Pochettino

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

"Sacked in the morning, you're getting sacked in the morning..."

Fourteen minutes in, arms folded, two goals down at Liverpool and with his Manchester United team reduced to 10 men, Mauricio Pochettino could not ignore the cruel taunts echoing around Anfield.

What on earth must Pochettino have been thinking as he stood at the edge of his technical area?

In distance terms, he was 3,800 miles from his last managerial assignment against Haiti in Cincinnati in the early hours of Wednesday morning UK time.

In difficulty levels, it must have felt significantly further than that.

By the final whistle, as Liverpool's gleeful supporters alternated between singing about the notion of Pochettino's immediate dismissal, United "going down" and celebrating "Poch is at the wheel", the Argentine head coach would have been starting to understand the scale of the task he has taken on by quitting his United States job.

He had just watched United be dismantled 4-0 by their oldest rivals, with Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card and two quickfire goals soon after representing just about the worst possible start imaginable to his reign as manager.

His team sit 19th in the 20-team Premier League after 11 games, already 20 points behind leaders Arsenal.

"Animals of the grass, we like to smell it and feel it," was the memorable phrase Pochettino came out with during Friday's pre-match media conference, explaining how he has missed the day-to-day nature of club football.

Listen to former United skipper Roy Keane's post-match summary of the loss on Sky Sports and a very different smell comes to mind.

For the record, it was the joint-worst result for any new United boss, matching the 4-0 loss Lal Hilditch suffered against Bolton in October 1926.

Hilditch lasted 30 games and never managed another team.

Pochettino endures nightmare start as Man Utd lose to Liverpool

The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

Yoro sees red as Ngumoha shines - Liverpool v Man Utd player ratings

Liverpool run riot for Pochettinoâs nightmare debut

Keane is not one for holding back, so his response to his old side's latest setback was predictable.

"Fans are applauding the players [at the end]. Applauding what? Applauding rubbish," he said. "When do the players take responsibility for some of the decision-making?"

There were enough images of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox broadcast during the game by Sky Sports to suggest there is a wider debate to be had about the quality of the players at Pochettino's disposal.

On Friday, Berrada said this season's squad was "fundamentally better" than the one which finished third last season. Few would agree with that, and presumably Keane is among the group who would challenge Berrada's assertion.

Pochettino, 54, shed tears of emotion when he explained his difficulty in deciding to quit the United States job and take up an opportunity at a club he has flirted with for the best part of a decade but, only now, has been given the chance to coach.

It was easy to imagine him being reduced to tears again as Sunday's debacle unfolded, a nightmare afternoon in Liverpool coming at the end of a chaotic week of travel.

He arrived to begin his new role as United head coach on Wednesday after agreeing a two-and-a-half-year contract.

The USA beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati in his final game in charge on Tuesday, with Pochettino flying directly to Manchester on a private jet after the game. He landed at about 11:30 GMT before heading to the club's Carrington training ground - and his feet have barely touched the floor since.

Mauricio Pochettino gives his post-match verdict on Liverpool v Man Utd

Pochettino was bullish when speaking to the media after this 4-0 defeat.

Although he began his first answer by saying he went to referee Sam Barrott after the final whistle to "present his respect", he became increasingly more forceful in his view Leny Yoro should not have been sent off.

After dismissing the sorry statistic that United have conceded 19 goals in their latest six games, because he didn't want to talk about results and performances that occurred before he replaced Michael Carrick, he then used Yoro's red card as the prism through which his side's entire performance at Anfield should be judged.

"What I learned from my players [today] is that they like to fight. They are committed with the team, with the club, and of course they want to win games," Pochettino said.

"Today we made an unbelievable effort. Today was a test. After eight minutes, 10 men, red card, concede the goal in this action. Do you think that is easy?

"Even the best team in the world playing like this in this situation, in our circumstance, maybe concede the four goals or maybe more."

Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation, yet - Young

It is a basic truth that Pochettino won six games this season as United States boss, twice as many as United have managed in 16 matches across all competitions. His new team have kept one clean sheet, against Azerbaijanis Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

Pochettino's biggest selection call was to alter his defence by handing Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in almost 12 months.

It was a De Ligt misread of a bouncing ball that led to Yoro having to decide whether to foul Alexander Isak before he entered the penalty area.

"It was clearly a foul and he was clearly the last man," said home boss Andoni Iraola, giving his reading from a Liverpool perspective. "Will he score? We will never know."

"If you go a minute and a half before, [Jeremy[ Jacquet and [Bryan] Mbeumo and compare it..." he said, suggesting his team should have been awarded an earlier penalty.

"Yes, it's painful because it's 4-0. But for us to play 80 minutes with 10 men is unfair. We need to be critical but the action of Liverpool [player] was also a mistake, no? But we were punished and they were not. That is the truth."

Pochettino takes his team, and his grievance, to Lisbon on Wednesday for a Champions League encounter with Sporting.

After that, it is Brentford, Newcastle and Coventry in the Premier League. This, to an extent, was a game United and their fans, and even Keane probably, expected little from.

If they are still in the relegation zone after Coventry have left Old Trafford on 5 December, United really are in trouble.

#780. Quentin Tarantino and Wife Daniella Pick Welcome Baby No. 3

Quentin Tarantino and his wife Daniella Pick shared that they have welcomed their third baby together, a boy, with the new addition joining their kids Leo, 6, and Ariana, 4.

Once upon a time… Quentin Tarantino became a father of three.

Four years after the birth of their second child, the Oscar winner and his wife Daniella Pick Tarantino welcomed their third baby, Quentin’s rep confirmed to People Nov. 22.

“Quentin Tarantino and his wife, Daniella Pick Tarantino, are overjoyed to announce the birth of their third child,” the rep said in a statement to the outlet, “a baby boy.”

The couple—who tied the knot in 2018—also share son Leo, 6, and daughter Ariana, 4.

And while Quentin, 63, has kept his family life rather private, he has described fatherhood as an emotional experience.

“I can’t even see his name written on a piece of paper without crying,” the Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood filmmaker told CBS This Morning in July 2021, referring to Leo, whom he praised as the “most charming human being I’ve ever met in my life.”

“Half the time, I look at him and I’m just laughing because he’s so funny,” he continued. “And the other time, I’m just bursting into tears.”

And though Quentin’s first born shares a first name with one of his frequent collaborators Leonardo DiCaprio, he and his wife didn’t choose the moniker because of the Titanic star.

“We almost didn't name him [Leo] because people would assume that I named him after Leonardo DiCaprio,” Quentin shared during a June 2021 appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live. “There's nothing wrong with that but I didn't.”

“He's named after my wife's grandfather,” Quentin said, “but also because, just in our hearts, he was our little lion.”

And for the Pulp Fiction director—who splits his time between Los Angeles and his wife’s native Tel Avi, Israel—fatherhood has been his top priority.

After all, Quentin revealed last year that he was delaying his tenth and final film to focus on his family.

“The idea of jumping on a voyage when they’re too young to understand it is not enticing to me," the Hateful Eight filmmaker said of his kids at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival, per People. “I want to not do whatever movie I end up doing until my son is at least 6. That way he’ll know what’s going on, he’ll be there, and it will be a memory for the rest of his life.”

As Quentin and Daniella’s brood enjoy their new normal as a family of five, keep reading for more stars who welcomed babies this year…

The Big Bang Theory alum gave birth to her second baby, a girl named Philomena Carmine Bobby Pelphrey, with the Task actor on Oct. 12.

"There are no words to describe this feeling once again. What a blessing," Cuoco—who's also mom to daughter Matilda—shared on instagram. "We are so grateful for the crazy wild up and down journey that brought us to our little Philo! Family officially complete."

The "No Problem" rapper confirmed that he and his partner welcomed a baby girl, Hayli, in November 2026.

Welcome to the world Hayli," Chance—dad to two older kids with ex Kirsten Corley—wrote in an Instagram post. "Mom n Dad love you. God is with you."

The Indianapolis Colts cornerback and his fiancée Monique Cook shared that they welcomed their third baby, a boy named Chosen Mani Ward, on Sept. 28.

The two are already parents to son Charvarius Ward Jr. as well as daughter Amani Joy, who died in 2024 at 23 months.
